summary: This informational document discusses using an Autonomic Control Plane to give network operations a stable connection to devices. Operations tools usually rely on the network being managed, which creates circular dependencies, especially when bringing up devices. An autonomic control plane can avoid that.

plainLanguage.summary: When you change a network, you risk cutting off your own connection to it. This document describes a way to run management traffic over a private IPv6 network inside the same devices, so that a mistake in the main network does not take the management connection with it.

subtitle: A separate IPv6 network inside your switches for management, immune to routing changes.

tldr.problem: Managing a network needs the network to be up, but the changes that break the network are often the ones being managed, so the management connection can be the thing that fails.
tldr.mechanism: The document describes how a separate control plane inside the devices, isolated in its own routing table and running on IPv6 with its own credentials, can carry management traffic that survives changes to the data plane.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational document that sets out the constraints such a control plane must meet and the options for deploying it, from a simple edge device to a fully autonomic network operations centre.

facts.label: GACP address family
facts.value: IPv6 only, using Unique Local Addresses

today: RFC 8368 is an Informational document with no obsoleting or updating RFC recorded against it, so it stands as the IETF description of how an autonomic control plane can carry network operations traffic. It has no IANA actions, and it deliberately leaves the specification of the control plane itself to the ANIMA working group's separate documents.

sections.title: The Circular Dependency
sections.content:
Operations, Administration and Maintenance, as the acronym is defined in BCP 161, is often subject to the problem of circular dependencies when relying on the connectivity service provided by the network to be managed. OAM can easily but unintentionally break the connectivity required for its own operations, and avoiding these problems can lead to complexity in OAM.

Performing OAM on a network device requires first the execution of the OAM necessary to create network connectivity to that device in all intervening devices. This typically leads to sequential expanding-ring configuration from a Network Operations Centre, and to tight dependencies between provisioning tools and security enrolment of devices: any process that wants to enrol multiple devices along a newly deployed network topology has to interlock with the provisioning process that creates connectivity before enrolment can move on to the next device.

Likewise, when performing change operations on a network, it is necessary to understand at every step that there is no interruption of connectivity that could lead to the removal of connectivity to remote devices. This includes especially change provisioning of routing, forwarding, security and addressing policies, which often occur through mergers and acquisitions, the introduction of IPv6, or other major overhauls of the infrastructure design, for example a change of an IGP or area, a change from Provider Aggregatable to Provider Independent addressing, or systematic topology changes such as Layer 2 to Layer 3 changes. All these circular dependencies make OAM complex and potentially fragile, and when automation is used through provisioning systems, the complexity extends into that automation software.

The traditional answer was to build a separate network. In the late 1990s and early 2000s, IP networks became the method of choice for building separate OAM networks for the communications infrastructure within network providers. This concept was standardised in ITU-T G.7712/Y.1703 and called Data Communications Networks. These are physically separate IP or IP/MPLS networks that provide access to the OAM interfaces of all equipment that had to be managed, from Public Switched Telephone Network switches over optical equipment to nowadays Ethernet and IP/MPLS production network equipment. Such networks provide stable connectivity because they are a separate network entirely, so change configuration of the production IP network is done via the DCN but never affects the DCN configuration. The cost is buying and operating a separate network, and that cost is not feasible for many providers, most notably smaller providers, most enterprises and typical Internet of Things networks.

The alternative discussed here is to get as close to that separation as possible without building a separate network. One of the goals of the IETF ANIMA working group is the specification of a secure and automatically built in-band management plane that provides stable connectivity similar to a DCN. It is clear that such an in-band approach can never fully achieve the same level of separation.
sections.plainLanguage: The problem is that the tool you use to fix the network runs over the network you are fixing. The old answer was a second, physically separate network, which works but is too expensive for most organisations. This document looks at getting most of the same protection without a second network.

sections.title: Five Constraints on the Control Plane
sections.content:
The document is not tied to one particular specification of the Autonomic Control Plane, but only to a set of high-level constraints decided early in that work, and it uses the term Generalized Autonomic Control Plane for any design that meets them.

VRF isolation. The GACP is a virtual network, a Virtual Routing and Forwarding instance, across network devices; its routing and forwarding are separate from the other routing and forwarding in those devices, which is called the data plane.

IPv6-only addressing. The GACP provides only IPv6 reachability. It uses Unique Local Addresses that are routed in a location-independent fashion, for example through a subnet prefix for each network device. Automatic addressing in the GACP is therefore simple and stable: it does not require allocation by address registries, addresses are identifiers, they do not change when devices move, and no engineering of the address space to the network topology is necessary.

NOC connectivity. Network operations centre equipment, which controls the OAM operations, either has access to the GACP directly or has an IP subnet connection to a GACP edge device.

Closed group security. GACP devices have cryptographic credentials to mutually authenticate each other as members of a GACP, and traffic across the GACP is authenticated with those credentials and then encrypted.

GACP connect interface. The only traffic permitted in and out of the GACP that is not authenticated by GACP cryptographic credentials is through explicit configuration for traffic to and from the non-GACP NOC equipment with subnet connections to a GACP edge device, as a transition method.

The GACP must be built to be autonomic, and its function must not be able to be disrupted by operator or automated configuration and provisioning actions, such as those of a Network Management System or a Software-Defined Networking system. Those actions are allowed to impact only the data plane.
sections.plainLanguage: Five rules: the management network has its own routing table; it uses IPv6 private addresses that do not depend on where a device sits; the operations centre reaches it either directly or through an edge device; every device in it proves who it is and the traffic is encrypted; and anything crossing the boundary has to be configured on purpose.

sections.title: Putting It Into Operation
sections.content:
Three stages are considered. There are simple options that the authors consider good starting points to operationalise the use of a GACP for stable connectivity today, which require only network and OAM device configuration. There are workarounds to connect a GACP to non-IPv6-capable NOC devices through IPv4/IPv6 address translation; these are not recommended, but if such devices need to be used longer term they are the only way to connect them. And there are options for the near to long term that can provide all the desired operational, zero-touch and security benefits, though a range of details still has to be worked out.

Simple connectivity for non-GACP-capable hosts. In the simplest case the GACP extends all the way into the NOC through one or more GACP edge devices. These devices leak the otherwise encrypted GACP natively to the network management hosts, act as the default routers to those hosts, and provide them with IPv6 connectivity into the GACP. The hosts need to support IPv6 but require no other modifications. Even though the GACP only uses IPv6, it can support OAM for any type of network deployment as long as the devices support the GACP: the data plane can be IPv4 only, dual stack, or IPv6 only, and it is always separate from the GACP, so there is no dependency between the GACP and the IP versions used in the data plane. This setup is sufficient for troubleshooting mechanisms such as SSH into network devices, network management systems that perform SNMP read operations for status checking, software downloads onto autonomic devices, and provisioning of devices via NETCONF.

Because the GACP addressing includes no topological structure that a NOC often relies on to recognise where devices are, it is likely highly desirable to set up the Domain Name System so that the GACP addresses of autonomic devices are known via domain names that include the desired structure. For example, if DNS has names for devices as devicename.noc.example.com and the well-known structure of the data-plane IPv4 address space is used by operators to infer the region where a device is located, the GACP address of that device could be set up as devicename_<region>.acp.noc.example.com, with devicename.acp.noc.example.com as a CNAME to it.

Four problems with this simple approach are listed. As a limitation, NMS hosts cannot directly probe whether the data-plane connectivity works, because they do not have direct access to it. As a challenge, NMS hosts need to support IPv6, which is often still not possible in enterprise networks. As a limitation, the performance of the GACP may be limited compared with normal data-plane connectivity, because its setup will often support only forwarding that is not hardware accelerated. And as a limitation, the security of the GACP is reduced by exposing it natively and unencrypted in a subnet in the NOC where the NOC devices are attached to it. These four problems can be tackled independently, and combining improvements leads towards a candidate long-term solution.

IPv4-only hosts. Most network equipment today supports IPv6, but it is far from being ubiquitously supported in NOC backend solutions or in the enterprise product space, so an IPv4-only management plane is still common practice. To connect IPv4-only management-plane devices to a GACP, some form of IP/ICMP translation between IPv4 and IPv6 is necessary, and the basic mechanisms are in the IP/ICMP Translation Algorithm. Two requirements drive the choice of solution: NMS hosts must be able to initiate connections to any GACP device, so every GACP device needs a separate IPv4 address; and GACP devices must be able to initiate connections to NMS hosts, for example to start NTP or RADIUS/Diameter connections, send syslog or SNMP traps, or make NETCONF Call Home connections after bootstrap, so every NMS host needs a separate IPv6 address reachable from the GACP, and the IPv4 source address seen by the NMS host must be unique per GACP device and the same address as before. Because of these requirements, the necessary and sufficient set of solutions are those that provide a one-to-one mapping of IPv6 GACP addresses into IPv4 space and a one-to-one mapping of IPv4 NMS host space into IPv6, which means that translation-based solutions are sufficient and preferred. The most flexible mapping scheme is the one in the explicit address mappings document, because it allows configured IPv4 to IPv6 prefix mapping. To be in compliance with security expectations, the translation has to happen on the GACP edge device itself, so that GACP security considerations can be taken into account.

Autonomic NOC devices. Setting up connectivity between the NOC and autonomic devices when the NOC device itself is non-autonomic is a security issue, and making NMS hosts autonomic so that they participate in the GACP is not only a highly desirable solution to the security issues but can also make the GACP easier to operationalise, because it minimises special edge considerations for the NOC. Supporting the ACP all the way into an application device requires implementing the autonomic bootstrap and enrolment mechanisms, the secure channel for the ACP, and at least the host side of IPv6 routing setup, and minimally this could all be implemented as an application and made available to the host operating system through, for example, a TAP driver that makes the ACP appear as another IPv6-enabled interface. If the structure of NMS hosts is being transformed through virtualisation anyway, it may be considered equally secure and appropriate to construct a physical NMS host system by combining a virtual GACP-enabled router with non-GACP-enabled virtual machines for NOC applications via a hypervisor.
sections.plainLanguage: The simplest version needs only configuration: put an edge device in the operations centre that hands out IPv6 addresses and gives the management tools a private IPv6 path into the network. It works, but the management tools in the centre have to speak IPv6, and until they do, a translation shim is needed.

sections.title: Choosing Which Path to Use
sections.content:
A GACP is not expected to have high performance, because its primary goal is connectivity and security. For existing network device platforms, implementing that additional connectivity with hardware acceleration is a lot more effort than without, especially because full encryption across the GACP is desired. Some of these issues may go away in the future, but it is wise to plan for long-term designs that do not depend on high performance of the GACP.

The expected answer is dual connectivity, through both the GACP and the data plane, between NOC application devices and devices with the GACP. The GACP connectivity is expected to always be there, as soon as a device is enrolled, but data-plane connectivity is only present under normal operations and will not be present during early stages of device bootstrap, failures, provisioning mistakes or network configuration changes.

The desired policy is that traffic between NMS hosts and GACP devices should prefer data-plane connectivity and resort to the GACP only when necessary, with the exception of an operation known to need the GACP, so that it makes no sense to try using the data plane. An example is an SSH connection from the NOC to a network device to troubleshoot network connectivity, which could easily always rely on the GACP. Likewise, if an NMS host is known to transmit large amounts of data and it uses the GACP, its data rate needs to be controlled so that it does not overload the GACP path, with software downloads the typical example.

Several methods can build up these policies. Ideally a NOC system would learn and keep track of all the addresses of a device, both GACP and the various data-plane addresses, and every action would indicate via a path policy what type of connection it needs, with a connection policy manager building the connection to the target using the right addresses. In the shorter term, a common practice is to identify different paths to a device via different names, such as loopback versus interface addresses, which can be expanded to GACP uses through the DNS or names local to the NOC system.

DNS can be used to set up names for the same network devices with different addresses assigned: one name with only the data-plane addresses, to be used for probing connectivity or performing routine software downloads that may stall or fail when there are connectivity issues; one name with only the GACP reachable address, for troubleshooting and probing or discovery that is desired to always use the GACP; and one name with both. Traffic policing or shaping at the GACP edge in the NOC can be used to throttle applications such as software download into the GACP.

Using different names that map to different addresses can be difficult to set up and maintain, and the name-based approach alone cannot strongly support policies for existing applications and long-lived flows to switch automatically between the ACP and the data plane in the face of data-plane failure and recovery. A solution would be host transport stacks on GACP nodes supporting a set of requirements: only the GACP addresses of the responder are required by the initiator for the initial setup of a connection across the GACP; the responder and initiator can exchange their data-plane addresses through the GACP and then build an additional flow across the data plane if policy needs it; and the following policies should be configurable on at least a per-application basis for TCP connections with GACP peers. Fallback builds an additional data-plane flow and uses it exclusively to send data whenever the data plane is operational, and when it cannot be built or later fails, traffic is sent across the GACP flow; this could be a default policy for most OAM applications using the GACP. Suspend/Fail is like Fallback except that traffic will not use the GACP flow, instead being suspended until a data-plane flow is operational or until a policy-configurable timeout indicates a connection failure; this would suit large-volume background or scavenger-class OAM applications such as firmware downloads or telemetry uploads. GACP only builds no additional data-plane flow, so traffic is only sent via the GACP flow, and is most appropriate for OAM operations known to change the data plane in a way that could affect connectivity through it.

Further requirements cover behaviour with peers that do not support these host stack functions, automatic rebuilding of a failed data-plane connection when the data plane recovers, including when a data-plane address of one side or both sides has changed, and end-to-end authentication and encryption of the additional data-plane flows using the GACP domain credentials, which may be skipped if the application already provides end-to-end encryption. Protocols like Multipath TCP and SCTP can already support part of these requirements, but how they can best provide a complete solution needs further work.
sections.plainLanguage: Most management traffic should go the ordinary way, and only fall back to the private network when the ordinary way is broken. For big transfers like software downloads, the opposite is better: hold off until the fast path works again, so the private path is not swamped.

sections.title: Why No IPv4 in the Control Plane
sections.content:
The GACP is intended to be IPv6 only, and the earlier explanations in the document show that this can lead to some complexity when having to connect IPv4-only NOC solutions, and that it will be impossible to leverage the GACP when the OAM agents on a GACP network device do not support IPv6. The question was therefore raised whether the GACP should optionally also support IPv4.

The decision not to include IPv4 was made for two reasons. In service provider networks that have started to support IPv6, the next planned step is often to move IPv4 from a native transport to just a service on the edge. There is no benefit or need for multiple parallel transport families within the network, and standardising on one reduces operating expenses and improves reliability. This evolution in the data plane makes it highly unlikely that investing development cycles into IPv4 support for the GACP will have a longer-term benefit or enough critical short-term use cases, so IPv6-only support is purely a strategic choice to focus on the known important long-term goals. In other types of network as well, efforts to support autonomic networking are better spent in ensuring that one address family will be supported so all use cases will work with it in the long term, instead of duplicating effort with IPv4. Auto-addressing for the GACP with IPv4 would also be more complex than in IPv6, because of the IPv4 addressing space.
sections.plainLanguage: Running both address families in the management network would double the work for no clear gain, so the design commits to IPv6 and treats the IPv4 translation as a temporary measure.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document discusses only the security considerations not covered in the solutions sections. Even though GACPs are meant to be isolated, explicit operator misconfiguration to connect to insecure OAM equipment, or bugs in GACP devices, may cause leakage into places where it is not expected, with mergers and acquisitions and other complex network reconfigurations affecting the NOC being typical examples.

GACP addresses are Unique Local Addresses, and using these addresses for NOC devices as proposed is not only necessary for the simple routing functionality but also more secure than global IPv6 addresses: ULAs are not routed in the global Internet and will therefore be subject to more filtering even in places where specific ULAs are used, so packets are less likely to leak and less likely to be successfully injected into the isolated GACP environment. The random nature of a ULA prefix gives strong protection against address collision even though there is no central assignment authority, helped by the expectation that GACPs will never all connect together and that only a few may ever need to connect, for example when mergers and acquisitions occur.

The GACP constraints demand that only packets from connected subnet prefixes are permitted from GACP connect interfaces, limiting the scope of non-cryptographically secured transport to a subnet within a NOC that instead has to rely on physical security, so only trusted NOC devices should be connected to it. To help diagnose packets that unexpectedly leaked, for example from another GACP that was meant to be deployed separately, it can be useful to voluntarily list your own ULA GACP prefixes on some sites on the Internet, so that other users of GACPs can look up unknown ULA prefix packets seen in their network; this does not constitute registration. There is a provision for address space that is not locally assigned, but there is no existing standardisation for it, so these ULA prefixes must not be used. PTR records for ULA addresses should not be installed into the global DNS, so operators may need to use a private DNS setup for the GACP ULAs, the same setup that would be necessary for using private IPv4 addresses in DNS.

Any current and future protocols must rely on secure end-to-end communications, TLS or DTLS, and identification and authentication via the certificates assigned to both ends, which is enabled by the cryptographic credential mechanisms of the GACP. If DNS and especially reverse DNS are set up, they should be set up automatically when the GACP addresses are assigned; in the case of the ACP, DNS resource record creation can be linked to the autonomic registrar backend so that the records are derived from the subject name elements of the device certificates, in the same way the devices themselves derive their ULAs from their certificates.
sections.plainLanguage: The management network is meant to be sealed off, and the private IPv6 addresses it uses make that easier: they are not routed on the public Internet, so stray packets are less likely to escape or to be injected. Anything that does cross the boundary has to be configured on purpose.

viz.caption: The five constraints a Generalized Autonomic Control Plane must meet

items.title: VRF isolation
items.text: The GACP is a virtual network across the devices, with its own routing and forwarding, separate from the data plane.

items.title: IPv6-only addressing
items.text: Only IPv6 reachability, using Unique Local Addresses routed in a location-independent way, so addresses are identifiers that do not change when devices move.

items.title: NOC connectivity
items.text: Operations centre equipment either reaches the GACP directly or has an IP subnet connection to a GACP edge device.

items.title: Closed group security
items.text: Devices hold cryptographic credentials to mutually authenticate as members of a GACP, and traffic across it is authenticated and then encrypted.

items.title: GACP connect interface
items.text: The only traffic not authenticated by GACP credentials crosses an explicitly configured interface to non-GACP equipment, as a transition method.
